🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -0.12% (intraday, 7-year +2bp). At trading day 22 (last close) it was -0.12% against a five-campaign average of -1.21% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.49%. The 10-year is +5bp since the hike vs a +17bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 2 of 4 signals: early signs of topping).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 739bp against a five-year average of 412bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +69bp and BB +51bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.30 → 0.62 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+8bp).
  • Bank Earnings: 8 banks reported (FFIN, INDB, SFNC, WAFD, CFG, MTB, RF, TFC); 5 red-flagged (INDB: NPLs +21% QoQ; SFNC: Coverage falling while NPLs rise (+9%, +$14mm); WAFD: NCO ratio +75bp QoQ …). Credit deteriorating at the margin; deposit costs flat. Watch: INDB, SFNC, WAFD, MTB, TFC.
  • Stocks: US stocks fell, led by tech; Europe and Japan rose.
  • FX: The dollar eased slightly; the yen stayed weak near 158 per dollar.
  • Technicals: S&P and Nasdaq slipped under their 50-day average but stay in long-term uptrends.
  • Sectors: Money left tech and media and went into energy, staples and utilities.
  • Credit/Spreads: Top-rated company bonds look calm, but the riskiest junk debt is under its worst strain since 2020.
  • Crisis: Moderate overall stress; oil and war are the main sparks, not banks.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is steady near 2.6-3.0%, but energy-driven prices are running hot.
  • Tech Bubble: Valuations are high but far below 2000's extremes; easy credit and markets look complacent.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Meta reports Wednesday; Bloom Energy's options price the biggest swing; US IPO pipeline is thin.
  • Iran: Tanker attacks and Saudi-Houthi fighting keep oil high; talks go through mediators.
  • Warsh: The Fed chair gives no hints. A hold is likely in October, with a hike still possible.
  • Week Ahead: Fed blackout; Netflix, Meta, Tesla earnings; housing data before Oct 27-28 FOMC.
  • Outlook: Short-term cautious; oil and high long-term yields are pressuring stock valuations.
  • Trades: Favor energy and staples, hedge tech, cut lowest-rated junk bonds.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 2 buy, 2 sell, 21 hold long, 20 stay out
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.60 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +91bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 93th pctile, +23bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: Rotation, not panic yet. Watch oil, the 10-year yield and junk bonds.

Friday's biggest story was a sharp rotation out of growth. The Nasdaq Composite fell -2.145% (-573.00 to 26140.03) and the S&P 500 fell -1.093% (-84.62 to 7659.44). The Dow held up at -0.336% and the Russell 2000 dropped -1.659%. US Info Tech lost -2.54% on the day and -6.37% over the week. Energy rose +2.47% as Brent climbed +3.51% to 109.64 and WTI to 101.41. VIX jumped 21.45% to 19.99 from 16.46. Sentiment moved from complacent to nervous, but this was not a panic. Europe rallied: STOXX 600 +0.72%, Euro Stoxx 50 +0.58%, FTSE +0.38%. The Nikkei rose +1.39%. So this looks like a US-tech and duration problem, not a global de-risking. The Treasury curve bear-steepened: the 2Y fell -2.99bp to 4.7083% and the 10Y rose +1.48bp to 5.0728%, putting 2s10s at 36.45bp (computed). That fits a market pricing a near-term Fed hold (Chair Warsh gave no signal in Bangkok today) while demanding more term premium for the oil and fiscal backdrop (budget balance -6.119% of GDP). Credit is the quiet story to watch. Headline US IG OAS was unchanged at 0.83 and US HY OAS stood at 3.21. Underneath, Bloomberg's quality-ladder data (as of 2026-10-15) shows the Caa–B gap at 724bp. That is at the 99.9th percentile of its 5-year range, well above its 413bp 5-year average, and the widest since April 2020. Is the CCC stress spreading upward? Partly. Single-B OAS has widened +50bp in a month and Ba +43bp, and the 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes rose from 0.37 a month ago to 0.58. Both point to spillover. Two things say it has not yet become a full contagion. The B–Ba gap (116bp) is still below its 5-year average (129bp). The Caa/B correlation is also still below its 5-year median of 0.70. IG has moved only +6bp in a month. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. Bottom line: an oil shock plus 5%+ long yields is forcing a de-rating of long-duration tech, and the riskiest corner of credit is already cracking.

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 489.91 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD is at 489.91 cents/gal, at the 99.9th percentile of its history. Every gauge in the set is at an extreme. The refining margin (crack) is at 104.3522 $/bbl with a z-score of 5.65, and the curve is in steep backwardation: front minus 12th month is 116.75 cents/gal and front minus 36th month is 205.85 cents/gal. That pattern points to a tight prompt diesel market where buyers are paying heavily for near-term barrels. Past episodes like this have tended to resolve through a fall in the front of the curve and a narrowing of the spreads, so the stronger signals favour selling, though the stops are very wide and show how violent squeezes of this size can be.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

Widening velocity, not level. The spread LEVEL carries no such signal once you control for already being in a drawdown (p=0.562) — tight spreads near a high are expected and are not reassurance. 💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.60 vol points (14th percentile of the 44 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 101.1 (73th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 90bp (steeper by 15bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (109bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 15 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 60/100 — Sticky but not re-accelerating at the core, with a hot headline from energy. The core-trend measures (median CPI 2.61%, trimmed-mean CPI 2.66%, median PCE 2.57%, trimmed-mean PCE 2.19%, core sticky CPI 2.78%) sit in mid-to-upper historical percentiles and are mostly flat-to-falling, as shown in the computed core-trend panel. Breadth is split: 28.9% of the PCE basket is rising faster than 5% (13.2% at >10%, 15.7% at 5-10%), while 25.8% is falling. That points to a concentrated energy and flexible-price shock (flexible CPI 6.12%, rising) rather than a broad wage-price spiral. Wages are subdued (AHE 3.0%, ECI 0.9%). The 1y breakeven at 3.01% vs the 5y at 2.39% shows markets see the shock as front-loaded. The risk is that oil above $100 bleeds into the core with a lag. Core PCE at 3.01% is still above target, and Wednesday's CPI was reported hotter than expected.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (41x) ≈ 24% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The bubble case today rests on concentration and easy credit, not on 2000-style multiples. The analyst estimates (not web-verified this run; the search budget was used on news) put top-10 S&P weight around 39% and CAPE near 38x. Market-cap/GDP is around 215%, which on aggregate measures is at or above 2000. Long-term EPS-growth expectations are elevated, near 70% on a 0-100 scale. IPO froth is modest at around 30, and the US calendar is thin. The trigger set that ended 2000 was Fed tightening, an inverted curve, rolling-over PMIs and credit cracking. Today two of these are partly in place: a hiking Fed under Warsh, and CCC credit cracking at the bottom of the ladder. The curve is positively sloped and the PMIs are still expansionary at 54.5 and 54.9. A week in which Tech fell -6.37% and VIX rose to 19.99 shows the market is vulnerable to a de-rating driven by duration and oil, not necessarily a bubble bursting. The 2000 drawdown template (-78% over 31 months) needs a much higher valuation starting point than today's 41.5x Nasdaq P/E.

⚔️Iran War

The war, which began in late winter 2026 under a fragile ceasefire, is escalating around shipping. Reports cite 10 attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz area in one week: six on Sunday and four on Tuesday. The Saudi–Houthi front is active. Coalition forces intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at Yanbu, and strikes have hit Houthis in Taiz; Iran denies involvement. On diplomacy, Trump told the UN he is deciding whether to make a deal or escalate. He has floated a strike on the underground 'Pickaxe Mountain' nuclear site while ruling out nuclear weapons and ground troops, and says the war will 'end very quickly' after the midterms. Iranian President Pezeshkian denies nuclear ambitions and rejects surrender, and Tehran called US negotiating efforts via mediators 'insufficient.' US officials say Iran downed at least two MQ-1 drones. The market read is a shipping-risk premium that pushes Brent to 109.64 (+3.51%) and lifts Energy, with a post-midterm escalation window as the tail risk. Details are fast-moving and should be re-verified against live feeds.

Sources: Al Jazeera – Iran war live, Oct 16 2026 · Fox News – Oil price hikes, Saudi-Houthi strikes amid Trump's midterm pause (Oct 14) · Fox News – Trump rules out nuclear strike on Iran (Oct 15) · CBS News – Live Updates: Iran's president denies nuclear ambitions · Sunday Guardian – Trump signals possible strike on Pickaxe Mountain

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Most likely a hold at the Oct 27–28 FOMC, with a real minority chance of a hike. In Bangkok today Warsh declined to signal rates and named the October and December meetings as the decision points. Futures priced about 15% odds of an October hike on Friday morning, down from 50% after Wednesday's hot CPI. Goldman reads a pause in October. Inference: Warsh has repeatedly rejected pre-signaling, so a surprise cannot be ruled out.

~1 YEAR

Inference based on his on-record framing: a hawkish, price-stability-first Fed. Expect one more hike, likely December per Goldman's call, then a hold while oil-driven inflation is tested against the core. He frames AI investment as an upside price force, which argues against early cuts. Inference from his long-standing prior views (not re-verified this run): a preference for a smaller balance sheet and less forward guidance, which supports higher term premium and steeper curves.

Warsh said the Fed 'removed a dose of accommodation' about a month ago, stressed that price stability is key, and called the AI development path 'very bumpy.' His refusal to guide is itself a policy stance: more meeting-to-meeting optionality and more rate volatility. Today's bear steepening (2Y -2.99bp, 10Y +1.48bp) fits the market pricing a near-term hold with a higher long-run inflation and term premium.

Sources: CNBC – Fed's Warsh withholds rate signal · Bloomberg – Warsh Boosts Market Expectations of Fed Rate Hold in October · CNBC Analysis – Kevin Warsh could surprise us all · investingLive – Warsh names October and December as decision points · PBS NewsHour – Warsh says price stability is key · NBC News – Warsh gives no hint about next rate hike
